Others, of course, are better situated, keeping lights which are near cultivated lands, or perhaps able to carry on some cultivation themselves. But I suppose my hon. friend has special reference to light-keepers situated at remote points like the Strait of Belle Isle.

Mi-. MONK. No, those on the south shore between L.'Islet and the Gulf-Father Point and other places.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I do not know whether my hon. friend is aware that some two years ago Colonel Anderson prepared a classification of the light-keepers all over the Dominion. Previously the light-keepers were paid to a certain extent according to the work they had to do and the importance of the light they had to look after, but there was no classification.
I think there is none today.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. Two years ago I had all the agents of the department and the inspectors of lights meet here to discuss the question of the salaries of the light-keepers and to provide for a classification. They made 16 different classes of the lights of the country. Formerly there was no classification at all, and there was considerable inequality in the salaries of the light-keepers. I thought it was a situation that was not at all acceptable and should not be continued, and that is the reason I got all the agents of the department and the inspectors of lights to come to Ottawa. They spent days and weeks working at the classification, and after they had outlined it, Colonel Anderson spent weeks and months completing it; There is no man in the country, I think who knows more about the lights all over the Dominion than Colonel Anderson.
Has each and every one of the light-keepers from Quebec to the sea been put in some class?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly. I do not know that the report has been asked for, but I shall be very glad to bring it down, and my hon. friend will see that all these lights have been classified.
I am not speaking of the lights but of the light-housekeepers. Does the classification govern the salary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Certainly. In each case I provide a minimum and a maximum salary. No one is appointed except on the minimum salary, and from that, if he is a good and faithful officer, he is entitled to an increase in salary.
Does that apply to the lights of the inland waters as well?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes. I know it applies to the Georgian bay.
Does it apply to the western lakes also?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I think so. I am sure that it applies to the Gulf, the Georgian bay, 254
the Great Lakes and the Pacific coast, and I am almost sure that it applies also to-Lake Winnipeg, though I am not positive. I shall be very glad to bring down the regulations and the documents asked for by my hon. friend. I entirely approve of what my hon. friend said in regard to the devotion of the light-keepers. I am glad to say that during the last six years that I have had charge of this department there has been only one case drawn to my attention where a light-keeper has failed to light his light at night. I think this is a remarkably good record. We are very severe in regard to negligence of that kind, and although this officer was well known to me, was almost a friend of mine, we dismissed him because we considered the interests of navigation at stake were so important that we could not allow a case of negligence like that to go unpunished. Considering the fact that we have in the service more than a thousand light-keepers, I think that is a splendid record, that during the last six years only one man has been found to fail in his duty on one occasion. I shall be glad to bring down the papers asked for, and especially the classification to which by hon. friend refers.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted, before this motion is carried, to add a few words to what has just been said. This question of the light-house keepers' salaries is not a new one to us, because I have done my very best, for five or six years, not only in the press, but also in this House, to defend that class of men so important with respect to navigation on the St. Lawrence river. I had understood, so far, that those officers were not remunerated according to the importance of their services. After quite a few years of persevering efforts I must say, to the credit of the honourable Minister of Marine, that he has taken their case in hand by ordering the officers of his department to study the question and to make a classification. I may say to the honourable member for Jacques-Cartier (Mr. Monk), if, however, he allows me to speak to him, that this question has been settled by a commission. A classification of the light-house keepers has taken place. I may think otherwise than the officers of the department on this question. While I would not say that they have been rather quick in taking action, still I believe that they have not sufficiently taken into account all the circumstances and certain details pertaining to that question. I think that the Minister of Marine might have this classification revised, because it does not do justice to all the keepers, I might quote instances; but I do not wish to take up the time of the House.
As a matter of fact this subject has been debated in the' press and elsewhere,.

and the minister has complied with our just requirements. At the present moment there are complaints of mine before the department and I hope that those requests shall be studied and that a satisfactory result may be arrived at before this session is at an end.
True it is that the sum of $50,000 has been put in the estimates with a view to increasing the salaries of those employees. That is all very well; but I would like to know how that sum shall be distributed. I could not say whether the honourable minister shall abide by the opinion of that same commission. At all events I would advise him to gather information with respect to each particular case, to consult people in the counties where there are such employees as light-house keepers, in order to ascertain who among those men should get an increase of salary. The importance of the light-house itself has taken as a basis for that classification. The difficulties arising from the very location of those lighthouses have not been considered. There are light-houses on remote islands challenging easy communications and lying far away from schools and churches, all of which puts the keepers to all kinds of trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
That has been taken into consideration.
Mr. GAUVREAU? Perhaps it has been, in certain cases, but if I could readily submit particular cases in which it has been completely overlooked. I do not wish to question the good will of the officers of the department; but, after all, human nature is the same everywhere, and mistakes may have been made. I will say to the hon. minister that there is certainly some discontent and that the classification made two years ago did not please everybody. One cannot always please everybody, and the hon. member for Jacques-Cartier knows it as well as I do.
At all events, I expect a goc*d deal from the efforts we have made on this point. I hope that this debate shall not be useless and that it may render some service to the so important class of the light-house keepers in the lower St. Lawrence.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in the debate concerning the question raised by the hon. member for Jacques-Cartier, and* I heard with much pleasure that the hon. Minister of Marine had decided to increase the salaries of the lighthouse keepers. Since I represented the county of Montmagny, I had occasion to go to the hon. minister's office myself, and to ask for that increase. There is a lighthouse keeper in my county, and I was answered that a classification had been made. But I do not consider that three or Mr. GAUVREATJ.
four hundred dollars is sufficient for a light-house keeper. When those appointments were made, old mariners were hired, men who used to earn a high salary. Now I ask the House: is it fair to grant those people who earned a high salary, men experienced in navigation, but who, owing to their age, were obliged to retire on a lighthouse in the middle of the river; is it fair, I say, to grant them but a salary of three or four hundred dollars a year? The classification has been made according to the importance of the light-houses. But it must be remembered that, previous to this, there was a system of pension for those officers, and that this system of pension has been abolished since; so that, now, those keepers have but this small sum of three or four hundred dollars out of which to make savings for their old days.
I speak for my county and as far as I am concerned, I am glad that this question has been raised. I congratulate the hon. minister who has'decided to take the question into serious consideration by putting in the estimates a sum sufficient to do justice to those mariners who were devoted to the extent of isolating themselves and whose important position carries with itself so much responsibility.

I am very glad to see the interest manifested in these men and I think there are same cases particularly where some measure of increase ought to be granted. I believe there is a petition being circulated to that effect at the present time.
Motion agreed to.

For a copy of a report by Mr. W. T. R. Preston, Commissioner of Trade and Commerce in Holland re the establishment of a Netherland Loan Company in Canada; of all communications between the Department of Trade and Commerce and any other department of the government and Mr. Preston on the subject-matter of this report; a copy of correspondence between Mr. Preston and any person or persons in Holland regarding proposed operations of a Dutch Loan Company in Canada, and a copy of correspondence or communications of any nature whatsoever between the government or the department with any persons relating to this question.
He said:	Just a few words with regard
to this motion. I think that all members of this House will admit that it is of the greatest importance for us to encourage the placing of foreign capital in this country. _ The motion now submitted to the House interests particularly the members from the Northwest because it is in the Northwest that the circumstances arose which gave rise to the making of this proposition. Some time ago there was a company organized in Holland having for its object to

loan money in the Northwest of Canada on first mortgage and to loan that money at the rate, if I mistake not-the correspondence will show-of 5 per cent. This was something unheard of in the west. As I understand, loans in the west, even well secured loans, command a rate of interest of 7, 8 and 9 per cent. The company sought information regarding the possible investment of a large amount of capita] in the Northwest and finally decided to organize and to invest, I believe, about $500,000 a year at the rate of interest that I have mentioned. As the preparations of the company were complete and when it had finally decided to start its operations, there came information to one of the directors of the company from some part of this country, I believe from Montreal, putting these possible investors upon their guard against investment upon the first mortgage in the Northwest and telling them, through this director, that the land values in the Northwest had been booming, and that they could not possibly have the assurance of a safe guarantee if they loaned up to fifty per cent of the value of this land. As capital, not only in Holland but everywhere else throughout the world, is extremely diffident and fearful, this information, in view of the source from which it came, deterred these men from carrying out their original intention of organizing a company and investing large sums at a low rate of interest in the Northwest. The object of this motion is to obtain all the reports, correspondence, &c., between the government and our trade commissioner in Holland regarding the establishment of the Netherland Loan Company in Canada, the correspondence between Mr. Preston and any person or persons in Holland and the correspondence of any nature whatever relating to this question.
It must be evident, I think, to the government and to the House that it is most important for us, since we expend a very large sum on trade representatives in other countries, to control carefully the reports unfavourable to the opening of trade relations which may be sent to the country in question where capital or other forms of investment are about to be provided for Canada or any part of it. It must be evident that cases will occur when rivals in business, men engaged in similar lines of business to those projected, or capitalists, fearing the rivalry of new capital arriving in the country, would be liable, if possible, to discredit and discourage the new enterprise. Under these circumstances I submit that we must exercise the utmost caution and carefully supervise any attempts of that kind that are made to thwart the efforts of our trade commissioners or agents who are sent into other countries in order to invite capital into this country. This is the first instance since I have been in the House in which a case of this kind has come up, and I suppose there is no objection to our getting down this official correspondence in order that we may see exactly what has taken place in the case of the Netherland Loan Company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, but for a fact that has transpired since my hon. friend put his motion on the Order Paper, I think that, for my part, I would have had considerable diffidence in granting the motion. No one can object to the statement which has been made by my hon. friend in support of his motion on the ground of the desirability that we should secure and obtain all the capital that can be obtained from every part of the world, and especially from so rich a country as Holland. I call my hon. friend's attention to this, however, that when the report came to us from Mr. Preston that the efforts of the company which had intended to invest in Canada had been arrested, as it was represented to us, by some gentleman in Canada, the question arose for us as to what we were to do. If it had turned out that the party who had just acted was connected in any way with the government of Canada or if he were any party for whom the government of Canada were responsible, it would be quite proper that we should obtain all particulars so that we might, if necessary, exercise censure upon him, or prevent a repetition of such an offence. But if the party turned out to be a private citizen over whom we had no control whatever, who was not responsible to us, who was independent of us, who could express any opinion that he thought fit, it would not be a question for us, and I think my hon. friend will see the propriety of the suggestion I make, that we should not bring down that correspondence because the opinion is that of a gentleman over whom this House could not exercise any authority whatever. Suppose this party, this gentleman from Montreal, as it is supposed by my hon. friend, had gone to Holland, and had got into communication with a party who intended to start that company and advised him, for reasons sufficient for himself, not to invest in Canada, this wuuld have been very regrettable indeed, the Teasons which he might have given would not be shared by any one in this House, but at all events, they were his own opinions and with reference to his own opinions, however, unfounded they might be, neither this House, nor, still less, the government could exercise any recourse whatever.
We asked Mr. Preston to give this information, on the supposition that it might be an officer of the government who would be responsible to us, and over whom we could exercise authority. The' . answer, which is quite the reverse of what we ex-

peeled, disclosed the name of a gentleman who is not connected with Montreal, but with the city of Ottawa. He is a private citizen over whom we have no control, and I think it my duty to call the attention of my hoir. friend (Mr. Monk), to this, and to ask him not to proceed further with the motion. It has since reached the ears of this gentleman that he is mentioned in this correspondence, and I have received a letter from him'to the-effect that he wants the papers to bp brought down and an inquiry made. When I mention the name of the gentleman referred to in the correspondence, I am sure my hon. friend will accept his statement; or the statement that he gave any advice of any kind in reference to the enterprise, is absolutely unfounded. I will read this letter now so that it may form part of the correspondence. I may add that but for the request contained in this letter, I certainly would have asked my hon. friend (Mr Monk), to withdraw his motion.
Ottawa, December 2, 1910 Eight Honourable
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, G.C.M.G.,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,-My attention has just been drawn to this day's routine proceedings of the House of Commons with special reference to question No. 4 by Mr. Smith of Nanaimo, on pages 4 and 5 and to notices of motion by Mr. Monk on pages 25 and 26, numbered respectively 8 and 9. I am also informed now for tbe first time that I am mentioned by Mr. Preston, the agent of your government in Holland, as tbe person who through some representations made to Dutch capitalists prevented the proposed establishment of a Netherlands Loan Company in Canada.
In these circumstances, may I ask you:
1.	To facilitate the constitution of the select committee asked for by Mr. Monk.
2.	To give me copies of the correspondence referred to.
May I express my regret that this matter has been allowed^ to proceed thus far without any communication with me.
I also presume it will not he necessary for me to add that the statements made by Mr. Preston, supported, as it is alleged, by some person or persons in Holland, are absolutely without foundation in fact.
Tours very truly,
(Signed) C. FITZPATRICK.
It will thus be seen that it is the name of the Chief Justice of Canada which is mentioned in Mr. Preston's correspondence. The Chief Justice denies in the most absolute terms that he ever gave any information of the nature that is mentioned in the motion of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk), and under such circumstances I dare say that my hon. friend will he satisfied that the Chief Justice would be incapable of any action of the kind referred to in the motion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: What I have just heard fall from the lips of the Prime Minister is absolutely new to me. I saw the report which appeared in the Montreal papers at the time and I thought this was the proper course to adopt, but I hope my right hon. friend will accept my assurance that I had no idea whatever who the person was who it is alleged had given this damaging information. I do not know if I correctly understood my right hon. friend, but I understood him to say that if the person who had done this thing was under our control as a government there would be no objection to this method of procedure; but that as the person is not under our control my right hon. friend does not see the use of pursuing an investigation into the thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Well, I do not know that the fact of the person being under the control of the government of Canada or not under the control of the government of Canada, makes any difference as far as this inquiry is concerned. It seems to me it is a fit and proper thing for the House, under all circumstances, to find out how the carrying out of the objects of this company was prevented. It does not appear to me to be different whether it is an ordinary civil servant who gave this information or a person who by his position is independent of the control of the government. The main object of these motions, and of the questions which preceded them was to find out the facts in order that in the future such things should not occur again, without any reason or justification for them. Does my right hon. friend wish me to withdraw both of these motions? I I do not think I could do that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With regard to the motion at present before the House, if the hon. gentleman wants to have it carried I have no objection in view of the letter of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. As to the next motion, notwithstanding the' fact that Sir Charles asks for the constitution of a select committee I have a great objection to that, but we will come to that later.
Does the letter of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick object to the production of this document?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick asks that it shall be brought down.

In order to get at the actual facts and to disabuse the minds of these people from any erroneous impression which may have been even accidentally conveyed, I think there should be an investigation, even if the person referred

to is one over whom the government has no control.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. D. MONK (Jacques Cartier) moved :
speechtext:
Whereas, in the opinion of this House, it is in the interest of Canada that any attempt to prevent capital from seeking investment in this country should be fully inquired into and prevented. That a select committee of the House should be constituted, with power to investigate all the circumstances which led to the proposed establishment of a Nether-land Loan Company in Canada, and the representations made to Dutch capitalists in order to deter them from such establishment, the person or persons making such representations, and the -grounds or reasons of such representations. Said committee to be constituted of five members, and to have power to summon witnesses, to employ a shorthand writer and to print all evidence adduced; said committee to report to this House from time to time until the conclusion of said investigation.
This motion is more or less connected with the previous one, and having heard the Prime Minister read the letter which he has just read to the House, it seems to me doubly important that this inquiry should take place so as to exonerate a gentleman of very high position who has been accused in the papers of giving information which was detrimental to the bringing of foreign capital into the Northwest. Although the representations^ of Mr. Preston are not well founded, yet, it might be of advantage to everybody to bring that fact out and to show under what circumstances, what has so far been called misrepresentation, has been made. Does not that appeal to my right hon. friend?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, and for this reason :	There has been a suspicion
that some person in this community had been guilty of having given to these capitalists an erroneous impression as to the character of investments, and the possibilities of profit which they could make. Nobody suspected that the person who is charged or reputed to be charged was the Chief Justice of Canada, and I feel sure that the moment it is known that it is the Chief Justice of Canada who is mentioned in that correspondence, whatever suspicion there might otherwise be will at once disappear. For that reason alone I would not agree with the motion of my hon. friend. There is, however, another reason. Suppose it appeared that Mr. Smith or Mr. Brown, a gentleman high or low in the community had given that information, he, as a private citizen, would be absolutely out of the jurisdiction of this parliament and we could not investigate his conduct. We have no provision by which we could censure him or prevent him giving his opinion in whatever manner he pleases, and I therefore cannot see why the parliament of Canada should be called on to investigate into the opinions of any private citizen. Suppose a private citizen of Canada were visiting Holland as a tourist or otherwise, and he made such statements, it would be beneath the dignity of the parliament of Canada to have an investigation into that matter, and it certainly would be ineffective. But, when it is a gentleman of the high character of the Chief Justice of Canada-and I take the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) without .any reservation that he did not know who was the person mentioned-it is another matter, and I am quite sure that had my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) known it he would not have made this motion. In view of the fact that the allegation is made in connection with a gentleman of such high character, I do not believe, that any one will for a moment think that we should have such an investigation. I hope my hon. friend will withdraw his motion.

I am in the hands of the House in respect to this particular matter, but it seems to me that the rule laid down by my right hon. friend, that in a matter of this kind we should only investigate the conduct of persons over whom the House has direct control, is not well founded. Because if we aTe right in saying that we must see to it that capital should not be frightened away from this country we have a right to investigate every possible circumstance by which capital has been prevented from coming to the country. I do not see that the matter of our particular jurisdiction over a person who makes the damaging statement has anything to do with the question. The object of this inquiry is not to punish, it is to get information of the statements and to show whether they are unjustifiable or not. There is no question of punishing the party whoever he may be who has deterred the capitalist from placing his capital in this country. I do not know what the correspondence asked for by the previous motion may show, but perhaps my right hon. friend will allow us to adjourn the debate on this motion in order that we may receive the correspondence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend might allow his motion to drop to-day and if, after seeing the correspondence, he wishes to renew it I would be very happy to hear it.

As I have just entered the Chamber, I do not know ex-

actly what has taken place. I have seen nothing in regard to this matter in the press or otherwise, except what is in the Order Paper. Is the conduct of Mr. Preston called in question in any way?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not at all.

Well, how did this suspicion arise? In respect to the chief justice I accept entirely the view that his statement on the matter ought to set it at rest completely so far as he is concerned. How did the matter get mooted abroad that there had been some representations made to capitalists in Holland which deterred them from investing in the Northwest? As I understand that would come from Mr. Preston.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is correct. A company, it is alleged, was formed to invest money in the Northwest, but aftdr haying gone to a certain length the capitalists withdrew and the company failed. It is alleged that the reason why the company failed to organize and to prosecute its _ undertaking was some information which was given to the intending promoter, by a gentleman who at the time was not known. Information was asked from Mr. Preston upon the subject and he was asked to give the name of the gentleman.
I said a moment ago, in the absence of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax), that the Department of Trade and Commerce asked Mr. Preston for this information in the supposition_ that the information had, perhaps, been given by some one connected with the Dominion government, or for whom the Dominion government had some responsibility, but it turned out, on the contrary, that it was supposed to be a private citizen and in the correspondence which was _ received, Mt. Preston says it was the chief justice of Canada who gave that information. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has written me to deny this altogether. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) asks us to have a committee appointed to investigate, not what are the conditions of finance in Canada, but who is the party who has given that information, that is to say, whether or not Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has given it. I submit that under such circumstances there is no reason at all to make such an inquiry.

The principle laid down by the First Minister that we have no right to bring before this House, or a committee any one^ except those directly under and responsible to this House, does not seem to be a sound one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How have we the right?
In many committees we often bring people before this House over whom we have no control, as for instance in

contested elections voters are brought here in large numbers over whom we have no more control, than we have over these private individuals. If in this case it is found, after inquiry, that what is presumed to be an allegation of fact in Mr. Preston's statement is only an allegation of fiction, would it not be courteous to a very prominent man to clear that up? I think it would. If there was no other interest involved excepting that it seems to me that it would be almost desirable to go on with the inquiry. I am not advocating that, but I am dissenting from the principle the right hon. gentleman has laid down that we have no right to bring before us any man unless he is under the control of this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We have the power, I do not know that we have the right to do so. I understand that this is a motion to have a committee appointed to investigate who gave that damaging information, if it was given. If it were a private citizen, I do not know that it would conduce to any good results to investigate and find out that it was John Smith or James Brown or any one else. I do not think it would be dignified or that it would serve any useful purpose to secure such information, but when it is now on record that the information was given by the Chief Justice of Canada, I think the word he has given is quite sufficient to show that he is quite incapable of giving such information.

If the motion is dropped,
and it beconies necessary to renew it, I presume I shall not be met with the objection that the House has already dealt with this matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Not at all. Motion withdrawn.

As against this information from Mr. Preston one of my proposed board of directors received information from a gentleman of influence in Canada that; first, farm lands in western Canada were held at excessive values
beyond the real value; second, these lands will after some time decline in value; third, at present mortgage moneys were available to the amount of 50 p.c. of the Value; fourth, at the rate of 5 p.c. interest per annum.

Will you kindly tell me whether the opinion given to me by Mr. Preston or the one referred to in the latter paragraph is really the most reliable? I want to see the company successfully established and therefore find it necessary to have confirmed information if I can get it on Mr. Preston's opinion.
In reply Mr. Fortuyn was informed that the representations made him by Mr. Preston were correct; and further that trust or loan companies in Canada to-day are obtaining first-class first mortgage investments on farm lands at 50 per cent of established values at rates of interest varying from six to eight per cent and in some cases as high as nine per cent per annum; that the department is informed by one large western trust company that they are only lending in many cases 25 per cent of the' actual carefully appraised valuation of their own inspector, and that the growth of the western provinces of Canada is proceeding with a rapidity which perhaps lias not been equalled by any other country in the world; that immigration is increasing; from year to year and the production of agricultural produce of all kinds is also steadily increasing; in fact the fertility of the west astonishes many otherwise well informed Canadians resident in Eastern Canada who perhaps have not visited that portion of the country; and that many Canadians in Eastern Canada are constantly visiting the west and upon their return express their amazement at the rapid growth of that portion of Canada.

1.	Are school lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta only disposed of by public competitions?
2.	What is the complete procedure followed by the government in order to determine the desirability of offering such lands for schools?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
1.	School lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are only disposed of by sale at public auction, except in cases where application is made by railway companies to acquire school lands for right of way, station grounds and other similar purposes of the railway, in which cases the land required for these purposes is disposed of to the company under the provisions of the Railway Act, that is to say, on such terms as the Governor in Council may prescribe, the practice being to have the land applied for inspected and valued by an officer of the department and then to seek the consent of the Governor in Council for the sale of the land required for the purpose mentioned at the price de-

termined on; and also in eases where application is made by boards of trustees to acquire the land necessary for school sites in school sections. In such cases upon the application of the trustees being endorsed by the Minister of Education for the province in which the land is situated the land, not exceeding four acres, is sold to the board at the minimum price provided by the Dominion Lands Act in such cases, namely $10 per acre.
2.	All applications to have school lands offered for sale are referred to the superintendent of schools lands, Winnipeg, who, after investigation, reports whether or not he considers it would be in the interests of the School Lands Endowment Fund to offer the lands at public auction at the time proposed, and at the same time suggests the places and dates of sale.
If his recommendation is approved by the department the consent of the Governor General in Council is then sought and upon it being obtained a list of the undisposed of lands in the district referred to is furnished the superintendent of school lands, who then has such lands inspected and valued for the purpose of determining the upset price in each case.
It is also the practice before holding an auction sale of school lands to consult the government of the province in which the lands are situated and to submit to the Department of Public Works of that province a list of the lands to be offered.so that it may notify this department of any reservations necessary for public roads or other purposes, and for any remarks that may be considered necessary.

In the case of illegal lotteries, or schemes devised and intended to deceive the public for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretenses, the power of the department is limited to declaring correspondence relating to such schemes not to be mailable matter, and to refusing to deliver it. 1.	In the strike of Grand Trunk trainmen during July and August, 1910, what effort did the government make to get a satisfactory settlement of the strike?
2.	What was the basis of the settlement so far as the grievance of the trainmen was concerned?
3.	How many of the men out at that time were reinstated in their former positions?
4.	How many have not been reinstated, and why not?

1.	The government from the outset offered its good offices towards effecting a settlement of the dispute and put forth every effort to secure the consent of the parties to a reference of the dispute to arbitration. The effort to secure a settlement by arbitration was not successful owing to the unwillingness at the outset of both parties and subsequently of one of the parties to agree to such a reference. The dispute was finally settled through the governments' friendly mediation requested by one of the parties and accepted by both.
2.	The basis of settlement is contained in the following agreement signed by the representatives of the parties:-
By way of settlement of the existing difficulties :-
1. The company will put back as soon as possible the men, other than those who have
teen or may be found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct, the understanding being that there is to be no coercion or intimidation used towards the new men.
2.	The company will put into effect from May 1, 1910, the rates named in schedule of rates dated July 18, 1910, those rates to be embodied in the present schedules now in effect on this line, it being understood that those rates shall in no instance effect a reduction in any existing rate.
3.	The company will, on January 1, 1912, make effective in train and yard service on the Grand Trunk railway the rates of pay and the rules contained in the schedule or agreement on that date in effect on the lines of the Canadian Pacific railway east of Fort William.
The three above propositions shall apply also to the Central Vermont Railroad Company, the said Railway Company to be substituted for the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the Rutland Railroad Company to be substituted for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company wherever the same are used or understood in the above. (In the case of the Central Vermont, by the ' schedule of rates dated July 18, 1910,' is meant the schedule issued by the management of that company since July 1.)
The company gave an assurance that by * as soon as possible ' in section 1 of this agreement was meant a period not exceeding three months from the date of settlement.
3.	It was estimated that about 3,450 men went out at the time of the strike. From representations received from representatives of the men it would appear that at the expiration of three months from the date of settlement about 3,200 had been reinstated. Others have' since been restored to the company's service.
4.	It has been variously estimated by the representatives of the men that between 150 and 250 men have not been reinstated. The reason for their non-reinstatement, as given by the company, is contained in the following words of a communication from Mr. Hays, president of the company, dated November 10:
In the opinion of the officers of this company our undertaking to re-employ all who were not found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct has been complied with.
The representatives of the men allege that the majority of those who have, not been reinstated have in no way been guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct. The representations of the men in this regard have been made known to the company by the government, and the president has undertaken to have each case that may be brought to his attention made the subject of special investigation by himself and other officers of the company.

1. Was the Minister of Labour a party in negotiating and concluding a settlement of the

recent strike of tlie conductors and brakesmen of the Grand Trunk railway, between the company and the men?
2.	Is the result in harmony with the anticipations of the minister, as entertained by the minister at the time of the settlement?
3.	Is the company, in the opinion of the minister, now living up to the terms and spirit of this agreement?

1. Yes.
2 and 3. The minister did not anticipate, at the time of settlement, that any difficulties would arise in the carrying out of the terms of the agreement reached. According to the representations received from the men, some of their number have not been reinstated in accordance with the terms of the agreement. These representations have been made known to the company by the minister, and the cases so reported are being made the subject of further investigation by the company at the present time.

What steps, if any, has the Minister of Labour taken to have the Grand Trunk Railway Company carry out its agreement to reinstate the striking conductors and brakesmen within ninety days, and particularly what has the minister done since the expiry of said ninety days to definitely ascertain whether or how far the company has lived up to its agreement, and to compel the company to keep faith with the strikers?

The minister has been in close touch with both the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the representatives of the men concerned in the recent strike, and has by correspondence and personal interviews taken up with the company all representations made to him as to noncompliance by the company with the terms of its agreement. The minister has also endeavoured to effect between the company and the men some arrangement whereby any existing differences might be left to the arbitrament of some third party. As the 'result of representations made by the minister and the government the president of the company has undertaken to have each case of alleged non-compliance with the terms of the agreement that may be brought to his attention made the subject of special investigation by himself and other officials of the company.
